source: Pople, Miller, Myers; in Clancey and Shortliffe (1984) ch.8, INTERNIST-I, an experimental computer-based diagnostic consultant
finding: The first large AI diagnostic program is a hypothetico-deductive loop. Findings evoke disease hypotheses, hypotheses are scored, then one of three question modes is chosen by how close the top rivals are.
numbers: Mode rule: pursue if the runner-up is 46 to 89 points behind; rule out if 5 or more diagnoses are within 45 points; discriminate if 2 to 4 are within 45 points. Questions come in small groups, escalating from history to exam to lab. Score uses evoking strength, frequency and import of each finding.
limits: Hand-built knowledge base covering roughly 70-75 percent of major internal-medicine diagnoses. Shallow causal model.
agent_relevance: Direct ancestor of our S3 generate and S4 test. The mode switch (rule out when many rivals, discriminate when few, pursue when one leads) is a ready control rule for the test step.

source: Pople, Miller, Myers; in Clancey and Shortliffe (1984) ch.8, INTERNIST-I evaluation on 19 NEJM CPC cases
finding: On 19 NEJM clinicopathological cases (43 major diagnoses), the program was close to the hospital clinicians and below the expert discussants.
numbers: Correct definitive diagnoses: INTERNIST-I 17, MGH clinicians 23, discussants 29 of 43. Failed to diagnose: 18, 15, 8. Total errors: 29, 28, 21. Only 19 of 42 screened cases qualified because the knowledge base lacked the diagnoses.
limits: Cases were chosen so every diagnosis was in the knowledge base. Authors name tunnel vision: it works one problem area at a time and cannot hold several at once.
agent_relevance: Early proof that a hypothesis loop reaches human level only where the knowledge exists. Tunnel vision is the same failure as anchoring in an LLM loop.

source: Miller, Pople, Myers (1982) INTERNIST-1, NEJM 307(8):468-476 (secondary report only)
finding: Search results and a bibliography entry describe the 19-case evaluation as similar to hospital clinicians and below the discussants. The authors said it was not validated for clinical use.
numbers: 19 CPC cases (same set as c02).
limits: Original article not opened; numbers in c02 come from the later book chapter.
agent_relevance: Cite c02, not this line, for numbers.

source: Kanjee, Crowe, Rodman (2023) Accuracy of a generative AI model in a complex diagnostic challenge, JAMA
finding: GPT-4 given NEJM CPC case text produced a differential list. The correct diagnosis was in the list in 64 percent of cases and first in 39 percent.
numbers: 70 cases. In list 64 percent (45/70). First 39 percent (27/70). Mean rank when correct 2.5 (SD 2.5). Mean list length 9.0 (SD 1.4). Quality score mean 4.2 (SD 1.3); older DDx generator 3.8. Scorer agreement 66 percent, kappa 0.57.
limits: Puzzle cases, not real encounters. Subjective scoring. Some information left out of prompts. Black box.
agent_relevance: A model can write a broad early hypothesis set (about 9) in one pass. Humans in the 1978 work kept about 4 to 5. Generation is cheap for an LLM; ranking and testing are the weak steps.

source: McDuff et al. (2023) Towards accurate differential diagnosis with large language models
finding: An LLM tuned for differential diagnosis beat unassisted clinicians on NEJM cases and also raised clinician accuracy when used as an aid.
numbers: 302 NEJM cases. LLM alone top-1 29.2 percent, top-10 59.1 percent. Unassisted clinicians top-10 33.6 percent (p=0.04). Assisted by the LLM top-10 51.7 percent vs 36.1 percent unassisted (McNemar 45.7, p<0.01) and vs 44.4 percent with search. 16.9 percent of cases (51/302) had some training-text overlap; no big difference before and after 2022.
limits: Text only. Clinicians did not use their normal workflow. Contamination possible for pre-2022 cases.
agent_relevance: Help from a hypothesis list raised human top-10 recall by about 15 points. A generate-wide step (S3) pays off in hard cases.

source: Brodeur et al. (2024) Superhuman performance of a large language model on the reasoning tasks of a physician
finding: o1-preview put the correct diagnosis in its differential in 78.3 percent of NEJM CPC cases and first in 52 percent. On 70 shared cases it beat GPT-4 (88.6 vs 72.9 percent exact or very close).
numbers: 143 cases: list contains diagnosis 78.3 percent (95 percent CI 70.7-84.8); first 52 percent. Before vs after training cutoff 79.8 vs 73.5 percent (p=0.59). 70-case subset 88.6 vs 72.9 percent (p=.015). Correct next test 87.5 percent. R-IDEA perfect 78/80 vs GPT-4 47/80, attendings 28/80, residents 16/80. Management cases: o1 median 86 percent vs GPT-4 42, physicians 34. Real ER second-opinion differentials: o1 exact or very close 65.8 percent at triage vs 54.4 and 48.1 percent for two physicians.
limits: Text data only; authors call for prospective trials.
agent_relevance: A reasoning model matches or beats physicians at generating hypotheses from sparse early data (triage) with no scaffold. A scaffold should focus on tests and updating, not generation.

source: Goh et al. (2024) Large language model influence on diagnostic reasoning: randomized clinical trial, JAMA Netw Open 7(10):e2440969
finding: Giving physicians GPT-4 access did not improve their diagnostic reasoning score, but GPT-4 alone scored higher than both groups.
numbers: 50 physicians (26 attendings, 24 residents), 244 cases. Score: LLM-aided 76 percent vs conventional 74 percent, difference 2 points (95 percent CI -4 to 8, p=.60). Time per case 519 vs 565 s (p=.15 to .20). GPT-4 alone 92 percent, 16 points above conventional (CI 2 to 30, p=.03). Final diagnosis OR 1.4 (0.7-2.8) ordinal.
limits: Median 5 cases per participant. Humans used the LLM freely, without trained prompting.
agent_relevance: A strong generator does not help if the human loop does not use it. The scaffold must force use of the hypothesis list; a free hand-off fails.

source: Savage et al. (2023) Diagnostic reasoning prompts reveal the potential for LLM interpretability in medicine
finding: Prompts that make the model follow clinician-style reasoning (differential diagnosis, intuitive, analytic, Bayesian) did not beat plain chain of thought; for GPT-3.5 the differential prompt made it worse.
numbers: MedQA free-response, 497 test questions after API errors (518 planned), 95 for prompt development. GPT-3.5: traditional CoT 46 percent, intuitive 48 (p=0.9), analytic 40 (-6, p=0.001), differential diagnosis 38 (-8, p<0.001), Bayesian 42 (-4, p=0.02). GPT-4: CoT 76, intuitive 77, differential 78 (+2.2, p=0.24), analytic 78, Bayesian 72 (-3.4, p=0.07).
limits: Single-turn questions with all data given, so no data-search step. Only the prompt wording varied.
agent_relevance: Direct test of asking for a differential as a prompt: no gain in GPT-4, a loss in GPT-3.5. Matches the human finding that the method is not what helps; knowledge is.

source: Schmidgall et al. (2024) Addressing cognitive bias in medical language models (BiasMedQA)
finding: Planting a cognitive-bias cue in a case lowers accuracy, much more for weaker models. Warning the model helps GPT-4 a bit and the others little.
numbers: 1,273 USMLE questions, 7 bias types, 6 models. Unbiased accuracy: GPT-4 72.7, Mixtral 51.8, GPT-3.5 49.7, PMC-Llama-13B 33.4 percent. GPT-4 worst drop 14.0 points (false consensus), confirmation only 0.2. GPT-3.5 average drop 37.4. Average drop across models: false consensus 24.9, frequency 18.2, recency 12.9, confirmation 8.1. Bias education on GPT-4 frequency 0.627 to 0.720; one-shot demo on recency 0.679 to 0.742.
limits: Bias is a pasted sentence, not a bias that arises during reasoning. Multiple choice.
agent_relevance: Outside anchoring cues hurt weaker models. A plain warning gives a small gain only in the strongest model, in line with human debiasing results.

source: Schmidgall et al. (2024) AgentClinic: a multimodal agent benchmark to evaluate AI in simulated clinical environments
finding: When a model must ask the patient and order tests itself, accuracy falls below static MedQA and the two scores do not track each other. Biased agents lose a few points.
numbers: AgentClinic-MedQA: GPT-4 doctor 52 percent, Mixtral 37. Interactions N=20 vs N=10: 52 vs 25 percent. MIMIC-IV: Claude-3.5 42.9, GPT-4 34.0, GPT-4o 24.0, Llama 3 70B 8.5 percent. Bias: GPT-4 52 to 48 (patient cognitive bias) and 50.3 (doctor cognitive bias); Mixtral doctor cognitive bias 37 to 29. Mixtral doctor fixated on a recent diagnosis and ignored new symptoms.
limits: Biases injected by role-play in the system prompt. Simulated patient is an LLM.
agent_relevance: Fixation on an early diagnosis appears in interactive runs. Halving the turn budget halves accuracy; the data loop needs enough turns.

source: Li et al. (2024) MediQ: question-asking LLMs and a benchmark for reliable interactive clinical reasoning
finding: Simply prompting LLMs to ask follow-up questions made them worse than answering from the first information. Confidence-based abstention recovered part of the loss.
numbers: Asking questions: 11.3 percent accuracy drop vs asking none. Abstention with rationale generation and self-consistency: +22.3 percent over the interactive baseline and +12.1 percent over the non-interactive initial setting. Still 10.3 percent below the full-information upper bound. Best system closes 51.2 percent of the gap in information-scarce cases.
limits: MedQA-style cases converted to dialogue; patient is an LLM answering from the record.
agent_relevance: A naive ask-what-you-need step can hurt. The test step needs a confidence gate (when to stop asking) to beat answering at once.

source: Hager et al. (2024) Evaluation and mitigation of the limitations of LLMs in clinical decision-making, Nature Medicine 30:2613-2622
finding: On real hospital records (MIMIC-CDM), open LLMs doing the full diagnostic loop were much worse than physicians, skipped guideline tests, broke format, and were sensitive to the order of the information.
numbers: 2,400 patients, 4 abdominal diseases. Physicians beat every LLM by 16 to 25 points (p<0.001); residents 87.5 percent, senior hospitalist 92.5. LLMs with full data 58.8 to 67.8 percent. Action-format errors every 2 to 4 patients; hallucinated tools every 2 to 5. Order effects up to 18.0 points. Only radiology reports raised cholecystitis accuracy by 16.5 to 18.5 points; only labs raised pancreatitis by 8.6 to 21.6. Only Llama 2 Chat asked for a physical exam consistently (97.1 percent as first action).
quote: LLMs are currently not ready for autonomous clinical decision-making.
limits: Older open models (Llama 2 class). Newer models are likely less affected.
agent_relevance: More data can lower accuracy, so input filtering matters. Weak models diagnose before gathering, the reverse of the hypothetico-deductive order.

source: Bani-Harouni et al. (2026) Language agents for hypothesis-driven clinical decision making with reinforcement learning (LA-CDM), ICLR 2026
finding: An agent split into a hypothesis agent and a decision agent, trained with SFT and RL, beats a prompted ReAct agent and its own untrained version on MIMIC-CDM, at lower test cost.
numbers: Mean class accuracy: LA-CDM 81.3, LA-CDM zero-shot 64.5, ReAct 74.9, SM-DDPO 37.0, OASST (from Hager, different test set) 54.9, SFT with all info 92.8. Average test cost: LA-CDM $1,295.61; ReAct about $185 more ($1,480.32); SFT-all $3,792.79. Hypothesis correctness 75.7 to 81.9 percent after training. Calibration error (ECE) 0.069 to 0.037. Picks ultrasound for cholecystitis in 64.9 percent and CT for appendicitis in 85.1 percent.
limits: Trained model vs zero-shot baselines. Only four abdominal diseases. Cost table row alignment read from PDF text; check against the paper.
agent_relevance: Nearest published implementation of hypothesis then test. The gain comes from training for calibrated hypotheses plus a stop rule, not from the loop shape alone.

source: Shen et al. (2026) Uncertainty-guided latent diagnostic trajectory learning (LDTL) for sequential clinical diagnosis
finding: On MIMIC-CDM a random test-picking planner scored higher than the prompted ReAct agent and the hypothesis-driven LA-CDM. Only a learned planner clearly beat random.
numbers: Overall accuracy: SFT-all 94.2, history only 54.1, history plus one test category 58.3, plus two 67.2, all info zero-shot 76.9, random planner 84.8 (5-seed ablation 85.4 +- 1.3), ReAct 74.9, LA-CDM 81.3, LDTL 93.4 (93.0 +- 0.4). LDTL beats random by 8.6 points and LA-CDM by 12.1.
quote: both methods remain below the random planner in overall accuracy on this benchmark
limits: Llama-3-8B backbone; one benchmark with four diseases, so random test choice is already strong.
agent_relevance: On small answer spaces, hypothesis-guided search can be matched by random search. Test any S4 gain against a random-test control.

source: Hsu et al. (2026) MedAction: towards active multi-turn clinical diagnostic LLMs, COLM 2026
finding: The authors examined 222 MedGemma cases (155 with errors) and name three failure modes in hypothesis-test loops: tests not tied to stated hypotheses, rigid or erratic belief updates, and lost track of the state.
numbers: 155 erroneous of 222 examined cases. Training on 32,681 synthetic trajectories (2,896 PMC cases) with a trajectory-consistency reward cut the share of tests followed by divergent belief updates from 15.2 to 4.6 percent, with about 13 percent lower cost per case.
quote: LLMs often adhere rigidly to an initial diagnosis despite contradictory evidence
limits: Failure counts come from one model (MedGemma); the fix is fine-tuning an 8B model.
agent_relevance: Gives three checks for our schema: each test linked to a named hypothesis, update direction matches the evidence, and a ledger of tests and results kept in the prompt.

source: Qiu et al. (2025) Quantifying the reasoning abilities of LLMs on real-world clinical cases (MedR-Bench)
finding: Reasoning models are good at diagnosis when all results are given and weak at choosing which tests to order; free multi-turn did not help.
numbers: 1,453 cases. Diagnosis above 85 percent accuracy with sufficient results. Exam recommendation 1-turn recall: DeepSeek-R1 43.61 percent; best precision 41.78 percent. Free-turn recall DeepSeek-R1 40.67 percent vs 43.61 1-turn; another model 38.22 vs 38.47. Reasoning factuality above 90 percent but key steps often missed.
limits: Test recommendation judged against the tests the case report happened to list; other tests may be valid.
agent_relevance: The weak step for LLMs is S4 test choice, not S3 generation. Matches the human finding that content knowledge drives the gain.

source: Wu et al. (2025) MedCaseReasoning: evaluating and learning diagnostic reasoning from clinical case reports
finding: Reasoning models often get the final diagnosis but cover only part of the clinician reasoning. Fine-tuning on the clinician reasoning traces raised both.
numbers: 14,489 cases. o3 10-shot accuracy 64.5 percent; DeepSeek-R1 48.0 (on NEJM CPC: o3 62.3, R1 43.7). R1 recall of clinician reasoning steps 64.2 percent. Fine-tuning: average relative gain 29 percent in accuracy and 41 percent in reasoning recall; MedReason-8B +31 percent 10-shot on the test set, +18 percent on NEJM CPC. Physician agreed with the grader on 84/89 checks.
limits: Case reports are published, often unusual cases; reasoning statements were extracted by an LLM, with a physician check on a sample.
agent_relevance: A training signal of expert reasoning moves results, supporting the reading that knowledge and trace content matter more than the procedure.

source: Tu et al. (2024) Towards conversational diagnostic AI (AMIE)
finding: AMIE runs a three-step chain at every turn: summarize findings and make a current differential, note missing information and confidence, then ask the next question. It beat 20 primary care physicians on differential accuracy in text OSCEs.
numbers: 149 scenarios, 20 PCPs. Better on 28 of 32 specialist-rated axes and 24 of 26 patient-actor axes. Top-k accuracy higher than PCPs at all k (p<0.05, FDR-corrected, 10,000 bootstrap). PCP differentials averaged 5.39 diagnoses (min 3).
quote: AMIE employed a chain-of-reasoning strategy before generating a response in each dialogue turn
limits: Unfamiliar text chat for the PCPs; patient actors, not real patients. Absolute top-k values are in figures not read here.
agent_relevance: A deployed pattern close to our S3 then S4 each turn: current differential, missing information, confidence, next question.

source: Nori et al. (2025) Sequential diagnosis with language models (SDBench, MAI-DxO)
finding: A panel of role-prompted agents around the same model improved accuracy and cost: one role tracks hypotheses, one tries to refute the lead, one picks tests, one guards cost.
numbers: 304 NEJM CPC cases. 21 generalist physicians scored 20 percent at $2,963 per case. GPT-4o 49.3 percent ($2,745); o3 78.6 percent ($7,850). MAI-DxO with o3: 81.9 percent at $4,735 (no budget), 79.9 percent at $2,397 (budgeted), 85.5 percent at $7,184 (ensemble). Average gain across the models tested about 11 points.
limits: Hard curated puzzles, no healthy patients, no false-positive rate. Physicians could not use search or colleagues. The gatekeeper is an LLM. No ablation of single roles was read.
agent_relevance: Best controlled evidence that an explicit hypothesis tracker plus devil's advocate plus test chooser adds to a strong model. Gain over bare o3 was about 3 to 7 points, with large cost cuts.

source: Nori et al. (2025) Sequential diagnosis, case analysis of the bare-model failure
finding: In cases where the scaffold changed the answer, the bare model anchored on its first impression and ordered tests that fit the current list instead of tests that most reduce uncertainty per dollar.
numbers: Example: patient with alcohol withdrawal who drank hand sanitizer. Bare o3 fixated on antibiotic toxicity and ordered costly imaging; the panel considered in-hospital toxin exposure.
quote: off-the-shelf o3 seemed to anchor on initial impressions
limits: Hand-picked disagreement cases, no counts.
agent_relevance: Names the failure the hypothetico-deductive loop should fix: confirming tests instead of discriminating ones. Rule: each test must separate the top two hypotheses.

source: Sun et al. (2024) Conversational disease diagnosis via external planner-controlled LLMs
finding: Letting the LLM run its own screening and differential questions fails for open models. An external planner built from guideline decision procedures fixes it, and light human refinement helps more.
numbers: GPT-4 Turbo (success/accuracy/F1): no planner 86/86/87; guideline text 98/73/79; extracted procedure (EP) 100/82/80; EP plus human feedback 100/91/91 percent. Llama3-70B: no planner 0 percent of dialogues succeeded; EP 100 and F1 83; EP plus feedback accuracy 91, F1 90. Intro cites that GPT-4 skin-disease accuracy falls from 70-90 to 30-60 percent when starting from scratch.
limits: Simulated patients from EMR data; few diseases; guideline procedures per disease.
agent_relevance: Disease-specific rule-in and rule-out question lists beat free asking. Supports precomputed discriminating-question templates for S4.

source: ACTMED authors, University of Cambridge (2025) Timely clinical diagnosis through active test selection, NeurIPS 2025
finding: Using the LLM only to simulate possible test results, then choosing the test with the largest expected drop in uncertainty (Bayesian experimental design), beat letting the LLM pick tests itself.
numbers: About 1,000 patients over three single-disease tabular datasets plus an OSCE-style multi-diagnosis set; five seeds; GPT-4o and GPT-4o-mini. ACTMED exceeded all baselines, even full information on diabetes. Implicit LLM feature selection chose almost the same features for every patient.
limits: Small data, structured tabular features. Exact accuracy values only in figures not read here.
agent_relevance: Explicit expected-information-gain test choice works with an LLM as the simulator; this is the formal version of S4.

source: Synthesis of c05 (McDuff), c04 (Kanjee) and c18 (Tu): list size, LLM vs human
finding: Synthesis line, no new source. LLM differentials run 9 to 10 items while the PCPs in the AMIE study averaged 5.39. The 1978 model said a few early hypotheses guide the search.
numbers: GPT-4 mean 9.0 items (c04); PCP mean 5.39, min 3 (c18).
limits: Cross-study comparison; the 1978 human figure is in the other angle files.
agent_relevance: LLMs pass the human limit on list size at no cost. The scarce steps are pruning and testing.

source: Synthesis of c12, c13, c14: random vs hypothesis-driven test choice on MIMIC-CDM
finding: Synthesis line. On the same benchmark family: Hager open LLM 54.9, ReAct 74.9, LA-CDM 81.3, random planner 84.8, learned planner 93.4 percent. Different groups and test sets.
limits: Cross-paper comparison is not controlled; Hager used a different framework and test set.
agent_relevance: The benefit is in learned selection and calibration, not in the hypothesis-test format alone.

source: Synthesis of c08 (Savage) and c19 (Nori): prompt-only vs structured agent panel
finding: Synthesis line. Asking for a differential in one prompt gave no gain (GPT-4 +2.2 points, not significant), while a multi-role loop with tests gave +3 to +7 points over bare o3 and large cost cuts.
numbers: +2.2 points (p=0.24) vs 78.6 to 81.9 / 85.5 percent.
limits: Different tasks (static MedQA vs interactive NEJM), so the contrast is suggestive only.
agent_relevance: Gains appear where there is an interactive test step and an adversarial role, not from a differential prompt.
